entry.title: Measuring Debezium Server performance when streaming MySQL to Kafka

link.title: Measuring Debezium Server performance when streaming MySQL to Kafka

entry.content:
Performance is a critical concern when implementing Change Data Capture (CDC) solutions in production environments. In this post, I am going to share how we have measured Debezium Server performance (deployed in a Docker container) while streaming changes from MySQL to Kafka. All of this with the default configurations for Debezium, MySQL and Kafka.

This post does not aim to compare Debezium Server with Kafka Connect nor to identify absolute throughput limits. Instead, it focuses on understanding how Debezium Server behaves under realistic workloads using default configurations, and whether it can sustain real-time change data capture in lightweight architectures.

It is also important to underline that, in this evaluation, the database is not stressed in a fully real-world scenario. Conditions such as long-running transactions or other complex workload patterns are not represented, as incorporating them would significantly increase the complexity of the test case.

Introduction

Measuring software performance is important. It directly affects reliability, scalability, cost efficiency and user trust. It is a prerequisite for making informed engineering decisions. Performance measurement transforms software from a black box into an understandable, predictable and optimizable system. It is well known that:

"What is not measured cannot be controlled, predicted or reliably improved"

Going beyond sayings and proverbs, performance measurement provides you with evidence to inform and drive architectural decisions. Specifically, performance testing can help you by providing information that enables you to:

  • Validate that the system meets requirements

  • Identify bottlenecks and limiting factors

  • Help ensure predictable scalability

  • Reduce operational and infrastructure costs

  • Deliver improvements in reliability and resilience

  • Build trust with users and stakeholders

Debezium Server

Apart from performance tests, another great unknown in the CDC community might be Debezium Server. If you are reading this, you probably know something about Debezium and CDC. But let me introduce you to Debezium Server. Debezium Server is a standalone runtime for Change Data Capture that captures database changes using Debezium and delivers them directly to configurable sinks without requiring Kafka or Kafka Connect. It addresses a common gap in CDC architectures: situations where Kafka Connect, Kubernetes, or large distributed platforms introduce unnecessary operational complexity. It enables teams to adopt CDC with minimal infrastructure while still benefiting from Debezium’s mature and proven connectors.

Debezium Server is built on top of Quarkus and the Debezium Engine. This combination provides a production-ready packaged runtime that can run as a single JVM process. It runs as a single process and although Kafka is not required, it preserves the core CDC guarantees:

  • At-least-once offset management (per connector)

  • Ordered event delivery per table (depends on the connector)

  • Snapshotting and streaming of the changes in the database

  • Rich metadata about transactions and schemas

[id=benchmarking]§ == Benchmarking

Now that we are familiar with all the components, let us dive into the technical details.

Starting with the hardware, we have deployed two EC2 machines in AWS of type "c5a.xlarge". Each instance provides 4 vCPUs and 8 GiB of memory, ensuring sufficient resources for both workload generation and CDC processing. We have called these two instances Observed and Observer (in order to separate the monitoring load from the machine where Debezium and MySQL are running). In the Observer instance, we have deployed Prometheus, Grafana and YCSB (the software piece generating the load). In the Observed instance, we have a single Kafka container (although it is not really necessary and could be substituted with any other target, such as Pulsar, Kinesis, PubSub, or even a custom sink solution), Debezium Server, and MySQL.

As per the preceding description, we are using several software pieces, most of which are already known, except for Yahoo! Cloud Serving Benchmark (YCSB). The YCSB tool, which was created by the Yahoo team and released into open source as of 04/23/2010, developed to evaluate the performance of different cloud serving stores. This is the link to their GitHub project: https://ycsb.site.

If you want to reproduce this scenario, it is quite simple. Go to debezium performance repo, clone it and cd into the infrastructure-automation folder and then run terraform apply. This will automatically create the EC2 instances, provision them with ansible (copy files and install docker) and start the scenario. Logging in Grafana will allow you to see how everything evolves and progresses (inside Grafana you will need to navigate to the MySQL Streaming dashboard).

With the technology stack clearly defined and reproducible, we can now focus on how performance will be measured and which metrics will be considered:

  • CPU and RAM Percentage usage: We are monitoring the resource usage from the Debezium Server container.

  • Network Input and Output: We are also taking into account the communications performed by the container.

  • Disk Reads and Writes: To check how much disk space/bandwidth is needed.

  • Throughput: This is the main value we are going to focus on (based on this value, we can estimate the operation latency) and we are comparing this to MySQL throughput.

For each of the preceding metrics, we calculate the average value over the duration of the test. Calculating the average value in this way, we arrive at a stable value, so that any spikes in the data do not affect the final result and are included in it. These are a few more detailed panels of the dashboard.

In the picture above, you can see a few of the panels related to the resource consumption. The two on top are related to the CPU usage, which is the calculated percentage of usage for a 4 vCPUs instance. And the other ones are the memory consumption in MB throughout the execution. The two on the left represent the evolution over time, and the ones on the right are the all-time average.

The preceding example shows the Debezium Server throughput that the test captures during execution. This throughput chart is split into two parts, a result that reflects the two phases of the YCSB test. YCSB executions are divided into two phases: an initial load phase that populates the tables, followed by a workload phase that executes the configured mix of operations. This behavior explains the two distinct phases visible in the throughput charts. If during first phase we observe that the throughput remains consistent with the configured level, we consider the execution successful (OK/1). On the other hand, if something in the process results in variable throughput, we consider that the execution failed (NOK/0).

The image that follows shows a detailed view of the second phase of the execution, which runs 300 updates per second and 300 inserts per second.

Results and Analysis

Let’s now examine the results to gain a clear view of how the system behaves under varying levels of load, so that we can identify trends that might not be evident from isolated measurements. If you want to review the detailed analysis, you can view the raw results.

With the preceding image in mind, let’s consider the meaning of each column.

  • TABLE_RECORDS: Desired table records we are going to work with in the execution.

  • TABLE_TARGET_OPS: Desired operations per second we are going to perform during the execution.

  • TOTAL_RECORDS: Calculated value, the value of TABLE_RECORDS times the value of TABLES.

  • TOTAL_OPS: Calculated value, the value of TABLE_TARGET_OPS times the value of TABLES.

  • RESULT: Indicates if the execution has ended positively or not. 1 means OK and 0 means NOK.

  • DURATION: Total duration of the execution. This includes both phases of YCSB, as explained above.

  • AVG_*: The average (throughout the execution) of the given resource. Resources: CPU, MEM, NET_IN, NET_OUT, DISK_WRITE and DISK_READ. Averaging smooths short-lived spikes and highlights sustained behavior, making it suitable for capacity planning but less precise for analyzing tail latency or transient saturation.

There are still a few hidden columns.

  • DATABASE: The database picked to run the test against. In this case it is always MySQL.

  • TABLES: The number of different tables we are using in this execution.

  • DISTRIBUTION: The distribution selected for the given execution. The examples cited in this post all assume that the data distribution is set to` uniform`. You can modify the setting in the YCSB options.

  • COMMENTS: A field for recording observations taken while executing the test.

Side note: these are only the values for Debezium Server container. We are not keeping the data for other containers, although we can see them in the dashboard.

The following analysis shows the results obtained from the performance executions, where the objective is to evaluate the system’s behavior under different load scenarios and operating conditions. This analysis focuses on identifying trends, bottlenecks, and relevant variations in the key metrics presented earlier. Let us look at the charts and analyze the results.

The chart that follows shows the execution time (measured in hours) based on the number of operations per second and the number of tables involved in the execution. The chart reveals that execution time does not follow a single uniform growth pattern that is driven solely by the number of operations. Although some table groups exhibit an increase in duration as total operations grow, but this behavior is not consistent across all tables. Several tables show relatively high execution times even at lower operation counts, whereas others maintain low durations despite handling more operations. This indicates that execution time is strongly influenced by table-specific factors rather than by workload size alone.

The next chart shows average CPU utilization. Notice that rather than scaling linearly with the number of operations, utilization varies across tables. In the initial table groups, CPU increases as the workload grows, reaching peak values at a mid-range operation count, after which it stabilizes or even decreases despite higher numbers of operations. For subsequent tables, CPU usage remains within a relatively narrow range, with only moderate fluctuations, indicating that higher workloads do not necessarily translate into proportionally higher CPU consumption.

CPU utilization is influenced more by table-specific processing characteristics and execution efficiency than by total operation volume alone. Other factors - I/O wait, batching or internal optimizations - might play a more significant role in performance at higher workloads.

Memory consumption remains stable across different operation counts and tables, with no clear relationship to the number of operations executed. Most measurements cluster within a similar range, suggesting a consistent baseline memory footprint that is largely independent of workload size. The following chart suggests that memory usage is dominated by factors related to logical database schema or to configuration, rather than being directly related to the volume of operations. The analysis indicates that memory is unlikely to be the primary scaling constraint.

As we can see in the next figure, network usage varies significantly across tables and operations counts, with output traffic being consistently higher than input traffic in all cases. In the initial table groups, both input and output volumes increase as the number of operations grows, indicating a clear relationship between workload and network utilization. However, this pattern becomes less consistent in later tables, where network usage remains high or fluctuates despite changes in total operations. This finding suggests that data transfer is influenced more by table-specific characteristics than by the number of operations.

Overall, we can infer that network utilization is a dominant and variable factor in system behavior, particularly on the output side, and can represent a potential constraint depending on table structure and data change patterns.

Our next chart shows how disk activity varies with different table and operation counts. The chart indicates that disk write activity remains relatively stable across most tables and operation counts, indicating a consistent write pattern independent of workload size. By contrast, disk read activity is minimal or negligible in the early table groups, and becomes more prominent only in later tables, where noticeable spikes appear at specific operation counts. One table in particular exhibits a pronounced write peak compared to all others, suggesting an isolated behavior such as increased flushing or checkpointing. This behavior is typically observed during log file rotation or log exchanges, where disk activity is driven primarily by the number of log files generated and the overall execution duration, rather than by the volume of operations.

As we can see in the next figure, the maximum throughput that Debezium achieves varies noticeably across tables, indicating the effect that table characteristics can have on upper performance limits. Tables 1 and 2 reach the highest values, demonstrating a greater capacity to sustain higher operation rates, while subsequent tables show a gradual reduction in maximum achievable throughput. This decrease is not strictly linear, as some tables outperform others despite their position, but it clearly reflects table-specific constraints, possibly related to data structure, indexing, or processing complexity.

The next chart highlights that the maximum number of operations per second is primarily driven by table design and access patterns, rather than by uniform system limits, reinforcing the importance of table-level performance evaluation.

But, what is Debezium Server’s observed upper bound in number of operations per second?

In this next chart we compare the relationship between MySQL and Debezium Server throughput. The initial peak observed at the start of the execution matches the value that we are targeting for this execution. MySQL fails to keep pace at such high values (1500 operations per second in 1 table). On the Debezium side, the throughput closely mirrors MySQL activity. In the lower panel, you can see that Debezium’s internal queue maintains a high and stable capacity throughout the execution, with no indication of saturation or backlog accumulation. Overall, the chart confirms that Debezium Server processes MySQL changes efficiently and in near real time, and that the throughput behavior is driven by the database write pattern rather than by downstream processing constraints.

Conclusion and recommendations

This study demonstrates that Debezium Server is a mature, production-ready CDC solution and a credible alternative to traditional CDC architectures based on Kafka Connect, Kubernetes or complex distributed setups. Throughout all tested scenarios, Debezium Server showed stable behavior, predictable resource usage and reliable change propagation, preserving CDC guarantees. The results confirm that Debezium Server is not an experimental or limited runtime, but a well-engineered product built on top of Debezium’s proven CDC engines powered by Quarkus.

One of the strongest takeaways from these measurements is that Debezium Server is particularly well suited for small-to-medium-sized projects, lightweight architectures and environments where Kafka and Kubernetes are either unnecessary or operationally expensive. Its single process deployment model, combined with low and stable CPU and memory requirements, makes it an excellent fit for simpler infrastructures, edge deployments and teams seeking to minimize operational overhead without sacrificing correctness or observability. In these contexts, Debezium Server significantly lowers the entry barrier to CDC adoption.

From a performance standpoint, the results clearly show that Debezium Server is not the bottleneck in the tested pipelines. Instead, the upper throughput limit is dictated by MySQL’s ability to sustain write operations. Debezium Server consistently mirrors MySQL throughput in near real time without accumulating lag. This confirms that, for the targeted class of projects, Debezium Server is capable of real-time CDC, with end-to-end performance effectively bounded by the source database rather than by the CDC layer itself.

With these results and conclusions in mind, if I had to make a recommendation to someone who wants to implement CDC in their pipeline, I would say the following:

  1. Start with Debezium Server and default configurations. For small-to-medium projects, Debezium Server provides an excellent starting point without the operational complexity of Kafka Connect or Kubernetes. The results show that default configurations already deliver stable, predictable and near real-time CDC performance, allowing teams to validate their use cases before investing time in advanced tuning or more complex architectures.

  2. Design tables and schemas with CDC in mind. Performance is strongly influenced by table-level characteristics rather than raw operations counts. Careful schema design can have a significant impact on CDC throughput and latency. Optimizing table structures will often yield greater benefits than tuning Debezium itself.

  3. Treat the database as the primary throughput limiter. The benchmark shows that Debezium Server can keep up with MySQL in near real time and that overall throughput is bounded by database’s write capacity. Performance efforts should therefore focus first on the database before attempting to optimize the CDC layer.

  4. Scale architectural complexity only when necessary. Kafka, Kubernetes and distributed CDC topologies are powerful but introduce non-trivial operational overhead. For lightweight or well-bounded workloads, Debezium Server alone is often sufficient and easier to operate. Adopt more complex architectures only if the scalability, availability, or integration requirements clearly justify them.

In summary, Debezium Server emerges as a simple, efficient and high-performance CDC solution that challenges the assumption that Kafka-centric or Kubernetes-based architectures are always required. For lightweight projects and streamlined deployments, Debezium Server offers a compelling balance of maturity, simplicity and performance, delivering real-time change data capture while keeping infrastructure complexity to a minimum.

What’s next?

While the results presented in this post provide a clear view of Debezium Server behavior under default configurations, they also raise additional questions worth exploring in follow-up experiments, for example:

  • Discover Debezium Server limits: Improve the architecture and configuration of this experiment to discover the load limits for Debezium Server.

  • Deploy Debezium with Kafka Connect: Run this experiment with a distributed and more complex architecture, using Kafka Connect to deploy Debezium.

  • Get involved with snapshotting: By omitting snapshots from our experiment, we skipped one the most important Debezium features. Snapshotting certainly merits further performance investigation.

  • Run different sets of workloads and databases: We ran the present experiment against MySQL and used a uniform workload. For a more complete assessment of Debezium’s capabilities, we should include different databases, connectors, and workloads in the test environment.

entry.title: Debezium 3.4.1.Final Released
entry.content:
As the team continues to work on the next development iteration of Debezium 3.5, we’re pleased to report the immediate availability of Debezium 3.4.1.Final, the first maintenance release of the 3.4 release stream.

In this post, we’re going to take a deep dive into the improvements and fixes in this maintenance release of Debezium, highlighting any features or noteworthy changes. As always, we recommend you read the release notes to learn more about all the bugs that were fixed, update procedures, and more.

New features and improvements

Debezium for Oracle

Dynamic Archive Destination Support

When an Oracle primary server fails over to a standby server, it’s very likely that Debezium has not read all the changes from the transaction logs on the primary when the failover occurs. As a result, when the standby is promoted to the primary, it will begin to write changes to a new archive destination.

When Debezium reconnects to the newly promoted primary, Debezium will attempt to locate where it left off, and fail to start. This failure to start issue is a result of the fact that the primary changes that were not consumed by Debezium exist in the archive destination specific to the standby system being in standby-mode, not primary-mode.

To solve this issue, the archive.destination.name configuration property can be supplied a series of comma-separated archive destination names. When multiple names are supplied, Debezium will gather logs across all configured destinations and perform a deduplication pass by redo thread and log sequence pairs. This deduplication pass will prefer logs in earlier destinations from logs in later destinations that have the same thread and sequence pair.

With this change, Debezium is significantly more fault-tolerant during a primary to standby failover and recovers without the need for a snapshot, as long as there is no data loss at the transaction log level between the two systems (debezium/dbz#1246).

Other fixes

  • Oracle: Recovery private redo threads can lead to LogMiner failures debezium/dbz#40

  • Oracle: DDL failure when user creates a table with a column named "override" debezium/dbz#1461

  • Cassandra: Returns wrong value for DATE columns debezium/dbz#1486

  • RedisOffsetBackingStore: Race condition causes infinite NullPointerException loop on reconnect leading to unrecoverable state debezium/dbz#1488

  • JDBC Sink: Fails to insert JSON data into MariaDB debezium/dbz#1492

  • MySQL: New charset not taken into account debezium/dbz#1504

  • Oracle: PDB name in lowercase not collecting DML operation [DBZ-9054] debezium/dbz#1057

  • MongoDB: Thread-safety issue causes incorrect source.collection metadata during parallel snapshot debezium/dbz#1531

  • Oracle: Log mining lower boundary does not update until a log switch debezium/dbz#1560

  • Oracle: Create Table DDL fails to parse when using AUTOMATIC keyword in partition list debezium/dbz#1566

In total, 11 issues were resolved in Debezium 3.4.1.Final. The list of changes can also be found in our release notes.

entry.title: Debezium 3.5.0.Alpha1 Released
entry.content:
As we begin a new year, the Debezium team is pleased to announce a new release stream for Debezium, 3.5.0.Alpha1. This release includes a variety of first pass improvements and changes across the portfolio, including performance optimizations for Db2, updates to Debezium’s Quarkus extensions, Debezium Server and Platform.

Let’s take a few moments to dive into all the details.

New features and improvements

Debezium for Db2

Control maximum timespan for change query

When reading the changes in a very active database with a large numbers of records, this can trigger query-resource limits such as CPU time. This can lead to the query being terminated prematurely, leading to a connector crash.

To address this concern, Debezium’s Db2 connector introduces a new streaming.query.timestamp.seconds configuration property. The default of 0 does not apply any timestamp restriction on the query, so it will continue to operate as it does today. So for most users, this is a net-zero change (debezium/dbz#1466).

For environments where query-resource limits are an issue, setting this value to anything greater than 1 specifies the maximum number of seconds for a streaming query to include changes for, noting that a value of 1 is not permitted. It’s recommended for most environments that require this behavior to start with 120 seconds and adjust as needed.

Debezium for MySQL

No longer fails for zero-year dates

MySQL can be configured to support the storage of dates using zero year format, e.g. 0000-07-15. When such values are stored in the database, the MySQL Binlog Client will fail with an invalid date/time exception, which will block the connector from consuming further changes.

Debezium will now allow zero-year values at the Binlog Client level to be passed to the Debezium MySQL connector without issue (debezium/dbz#1499).

Debezium for Oracle

Dynamic Archive Destination Support

When an Oracle primary server fails over to a standby server, it’s very likely that Debezium has not read all the changes from the transaction logs on the primary when the failover occurs. As a result, when the standby is promoted to the primary, it will begin to write changes to a new archive destination.

When Debezium reconnects to the newly promoted primary, Debezium will attempt to locate where it left off, and fail to start. This failure to start issue is a result of the fact that the primary changes that were not consumed by Debezium exist in the archive destination specific to the standby system being in standby-mode, not primary-mode.

To solve this issue, the archive.destination.name configuration property can be supplied a series of comma-separated archive destination names. When multiple names are supplied, Debezium will gather logs across all configured destinations and perform a deduplication pass by redo thread and log sequence pairs. This deduplication pass will prefer logs in earlier destinations from logs in later destinations that have the same thread and sequence pair.

With this change, Debezium is significantly more fault-tolerant during a primary to standby failover and recovers without the need for a snapshot, as long as there is no data loss at the transaction log level between the two systems (debezium/dbz#1246).

Debezium Quarkus Extensions

Extensions relocated

One of the biggest changes in Debezium 3.5 is the relocation of the Debezium Quarkus extensions, which includes both the connector and outbox extensions. All of Debezium’s Quarkus-related modules are now found in the Debezium Quarkus repository.

All artifacts previously released in Debezium 3.4 using the quarkus-debezium-XYZ naming convention have been renamed. Please be sure to update your dependencies to reflect the artifacts named as debezium-quarkus-XYZ. The dependency groupId was unchanged.

In a future build, the Debezium Quarkus Extensions will be unbundled from the main Debezium release pipeline, and instead will be released with a similar cadence to the upstream Quarkus project. This will provide an improved parity between extension changes and Quarkus releases.

Support for Db2

The Debezium Quarkus extensions also now include an implementation for Debezium’s Db2 connector (debezium/dbz#1447). In a Quarkus application that uses Db2, developers can now respond to real-time changes by simply including the new Db2 module:

Debezium Db2 extension maven coordinates
<dependency>
  <groupId>io.debezium.quarkus</groupId>
  <artifactId>debezium-quarkus-db2</artifactId>
  <version>v3.5.0.Alpha1</version>
</dependency>

JBang Support

Debezium introduces JBang support by introducing an easy way to integrate Debezium’s Quarkus extensions (debezium/dbz#1464). This support requires Java 21 or later, JBang 0.132.1 or later, and a containerized environment for local services.

To get started quickly, the Debezium JBang catalog needs to be added.

There are templates available for the following data sources: postgres, mysql, mongodb, sqlserver, mariadb. There will be additional data sources added over time.

Debezium Platform

Support for HTTPS-based URLs

Users who may be using HTTPS via Traefik, ALB, or similar tooling, the current Helm chart setup lead to a series of errors when using secure connections. To provide TLS-based connectivity, the following configuration options were introduced (debezium/dbz#36):

Table 1. New Helm charts configuration properties
Property Description Default

domain.name

Represents the domain used as ingress host

""

ingress.enabled

Enable ingress resource for conductor/stage

true

ingress.className

Optional ingress class name

"""

ingress.annotations

Extra ingress annotations

{}

ingress.tls.enabled

Enable TLS section on ingress

false

ingress.tls.secretName

Secret name used when TLS is enabled

""

There are also some deprecated configuration properties.

Table 2. Deprecated Helm charts configuration properties
Property Description Default

domain.url

This was replaced by domain.name

""

Debezium Server

Jetstream retries on failures

Currently, when Debezium Server publishes to NATS and the queue is full due to some limitations like message or byte limits, Debezium Server currently throws an exception and terminates. In order to make integration with NATs more fault tolerant, the following additional configuration options have been introduced, allowing the Jetstream NATS adapter to handle retries natively (debezium/dbz#1494):

Table 3. New configuration property for NATS Jetstream adapter
Property Description Default

sync.retries

Specifies the number of retries

5

sync.retry.interval.ms

The number of milliseconds to wait between retries.

1000

sync.retry.max.interval.ms

The maximum number of milliseconds to wait between retries.

60000

sync.retry.backoff.multiplier

The back-off multiplier to scale the retry interval over attempts.

2.0

All configuration options should be prefixed with debezium.sink.nats-jetstream.

Other changes

  • Recovery private redo threads can lead to LogMiner failures debezium/dbz#40

  • On adding "Signalling collection name" in the Form editor it should by preserved in the smart editor [DBZ-9080] debezium/dbz#1226

  • Update Debezium Platform doc with recent features [DBZ-9319] debezium/dbz#1381

  • Platform: UI Bugs [DBZ-9559] debezium/dbz#1416

  • Deleting pipeline does not work when pressing enter after typing name [DBZ-9687] debezium/dbz#1436

  • Oracle connector fails when user creates a table with a column named "override" debezium/dbz#1461

  • Debezium-Platform: Fix The grep notification feature in the pipeline logs debezium/dbz#1465

  • remove unnecessary jbang main() debezium/dbz#1467

  • introduce a factory for io.debezium.runtime.Debezium debezium/dbz#1469

  • Debezium Server: HTTP sink, JWTAuthenticatorTests fail debezium/dbz#1470

  • Debezium issue on connect to IBMi debezium/dbz#1473

  • Oracle OLR adapter crashes with auto-commit error when encountering unknown tables debezium/dbz#1480

  • Impossible to run docker image for testing purpose with docker-maven-plugin and docker API version > 1.44 debezium/dbz#1481

  • Cassandra connector return wrong value for DATE columns debezium/dbz#1486

  • RedisOffsetBackingStore: Race condition causes infinite NullPointerException loop on reconnect leading to unrecoverable state debezium/dbz#1488

  • pg_stat_replication.flush_lsn can move backwards when lsn.flush.mode=connector_and_driver debezium/dbz#1489

  • JDBC Sink Connector fails to insert JSON data into MariaDB debezium/dbz#1492

  • Refactor OracleConnection auto-commit setup as an initial Operation debezium/dbz#1496

  • Connector cannot handle uncompressed transaction payloads beyond 2GB debezium/dbz#1503

  • MySQL: New charset not taken into account debezium/dbz#1504

  • Debezium Platrform: Update the source and destination flow to get the connections details in smart editor. debezium/dbz#1506

  • add debezium-quarkus project in debezium-platform-conductor pipeline debezium/dbz#1507

  • Add debezium platform conductor into core CI debezium/dbz#1520

  • DCO must be checked only on pull request debezium/dbz#1524

  • ReselectPostProcessor does not account for CustomConverter(s) debezium/dbz#1527

  • Thread-safety issue in MongoDB connector causes incorrect source.collection metadata during parallel snapshot debezium/dbz#1531

Summary

In total, 44 issues were resolved in Debezium 3.5.0.Alpha1. The list of changes can also be found in our release notes.

A big thank you to all the contributors from the community who worked diligently on this release:
Anton Repin, Alexandre Busquets, Atsushi Torikoshi, Chris Cranford, Conor Gallagher, Giovanni Panice, Haydar, Haydar Miezanie Abdul Jamil, Haydar Miezanie Abdul Jamil, Indra Shukla, Jiri Pechanec, Maarten Vercruysse, Mario Fiore Vitale, Mateusz Tworek, Matt Hejnas, Nicolas Payart, Olivier Chédru, Rophy Tsai, Rudi Bruchez, sreedev, Vojtech Juranek

entry.title: LLMs in the Loop: Using AI to Migrate JUnit Tests

link.title: LLMs in the Loop: Using AI to Migrate JUnit Tests

entry.content:
JUnit 5 was released in late 2017, and since then the migration from JUnit 4 has been written about extensively, so much so that, at first glance, it may feel like an old and well-trodden topic.

JUnit usage statistics

Yet in reality, the chart makes it clear that JUnit 4 is still very much alive in the ecosystem. According to Libraries.io, JUnit 4 has 91.5K dependent packages and 29.3K dependent repositories. By comparison, JUnit 5’s junit-jupiter-engine has only 20.8K dependent packages and 5.3K dependent repositories.

Clearly, there are still many projects running on JUnit 4 today.

The reasons can vary, but in my experience the most common ones are:

  • JUnit 5 introduced the possibility of running existing JUnit 4 tests via the junit-vintage engine. The idea was to allow users to temporarily keep running old tests on the new jupiter engine and migrate incrementally.

  • Migration is a time-consuming task. (It fits perfectly in any long-lived tech debt list :))

  • The tests work. Don’t touch them.

Regarding junit-vintage, I don’t think the original expectation was for this temporary period to last this long. That phase now appears to be approaching its end, as suggested by the JUnit 6 release notes, where a deprecation notice states:

The JUnit Vintage engine is now deprecated and will report an INFO level discovery issue when it finds at least one JUnit 4 test class. For now, the intent of the deprecation is not to signal removal in the next major version but to clarify the intended purpose of the engine. It should only be used temporarily while migrating tests to JUnit Jupiter or another testing framework with native JUnit Platform support.

To be honest I just discovered this deprecation notice while writing this article. For us, the real motivation was a combination of all the points above, amplified by a very large test suite and limited team capacity.

Within the Debezium team, we’ve been aware of this technical debt for years. We discussed it multiple times and even sketched out plans, but priorities kept shifting—as they often do.

Recently, the topic came up again in a discussion this time driven by Quarkus 3.31 adding support for JUnit 6.

Around the same time, I had been experimenting with Claude Code and thought: why not use it here?

In this article, I’ll walk through the migration process, explain how we approached it, and share what worked—and what didn’t—along the way.

Before the migration, the Debezium test suite was still largely based on JUnit 4. The distribution of test files across JUnit 4 and JUnit 5 is shown in the chart below:

Debezium JUnit stats

The chart makes it clear: JUnit 4 was still deeply entrenched in the project, which explains why a fully manual migration would have been slow, error-prone, and difficult to sustain.

About the JUnit migration

In the years following the introduction of JUnit 5, and as users gained experience with the migration from JUnit 4, a fairly well-defined high-level recipe emerged.

JUnit 4 to JUnit 5 migration recipe

  • Update dependencies to JUnit Jupiter

  • Change imports from org.junit. to org.junit.jupiter.api.

  • Update lifecycle annotations (@Before → @BeforeEach, @BeforeClass → @BeforeAll, etc.)

  • Migrate Rules to Extensions (@Rule → @ExtendWith)

Thanks to these clearly defined rules, I had already come across a dedicated JUnit 5 migration recipe for OpenRewrite:

However, for the reasons described earlier, we never seriously approached the migration.

Since then, things have changed a bit. AI, and in particular GenAI, has started to show up everywhere.

For me, this felt like an almost ideal task for an LLM: a clear set of rules applied repeatedly to a large codebase.

AI Augmented approach

I recently started using Claude Code during my daily work to help me:

  • investigating and fixing bugs

  • writing tests

  • challenging my design choices

It doesn’t always help, but in some cases it has genuinely helped me avoid mistakes or resolve issues more quickly.

So, why not try it here?

I don’t recall the exact prompt I used, but the idea was to ask Claude to analyze the codebase and provide an overview of the changes needed for the migration. I’m pretty sure I used the word plan, because Claude immediately switched into plan mode.

At the time, I wasn’t aware this mode even existed, so I checked the Claude Code documentation, which describes it as:

Plan Mode instructs Claude to create a plan by analyzing the codebase with read-only operations, perfect for exploring codebases, planning complex changes, or reviewing code safely.

The documentation also suggests using plan mode in the following situations:

  • Multi-step implementation: When your feature requires making edits to many files

  • Code exploration: When you want to research the codebase thoroughly before changing anything

  • Interactive development: When you want to iterate on the direction with Claude

This was exactly what I was looking for. Claude also asked a few questions about the possible approaches to use during the migration. After some back and forth, it proposed the following Executive Summary.

This plan details a phased, module-by-module migration of the Debezium codebase from JUnit 4 to JUnit 5. The migration will use a hybrid approach where JUnit 5 Extensions are created alongside existing JUnit 4 Rules, allowing both to coexist during the transition. The migration will start with core modules and progress through connector modules in dependency order.

Key Stats:
- 384+ test files using JUnit 4 (100% of tests)
- ~95 Maven modules in the project
- JUnit 5.9.1 already in BOM with vintage engine available
- All test dependencies (Mockito 5.19.0, AssertJ 3.27.5, TestContainers 2.0.2) are JUnit 5 compatible

Migration Approach:
- Strategy: Phased module-by-module migration
- Custom Rules: Hybrid approach - create JUnit 5 Extensions alongside existing Rules
- Priority: Start with core modules (debezium-core and shared infrastructure)
- Scope: Minimal changes - JUnit 5 migration only, no additional modernization

You can find the full and detailed plan here

I accepted the plan and asked Claude Code to start implementing it. The way it worked was exactly how a software engineer would expect it: apply a change, verify that the code still compiles, and then move on to the next step. Once a module was completed, it didn’t just stop at compilation—it also verified that the tests were actually passing.

Claude working on code changes

I don’t have the exact number of hours the process took, but in roughly one working day (split into two half-days) I was able to open the final pull request.

It worked. In just one day, we migrated the entire test suite to JUnit 5.

That said, the process was not completely hands-off. I had to supervise it and occasionally provide more specific prompts to address issues. For example, Claude initially claimed that the codebase no longer depended on JUnit 4, while I could still see old JUnit imports. After being nudged, it correctly identified a transitive dependency as the source.

In other cases, assertions were mechanically migrated by renaming methods, but without adjusting the order of parameters, causing some tests to fail. Finally, there were a few manual changes needed to fix test isolation issues that only surfaced under the JUnit 5 engine, which executes tests in a different order compared to JUnit 4.

Apart from these cases, the process was surprisingly smooth. For the most part, I just supervised it while working on other tasks.

Conclusion

We finally removed a technical debt, and for me, that is the most important part, how we did it comes second. This was also the perfect occasion to “test” GenAI on a real problem, and we can fairly say that it worked.

I know the question you’re probably repeating in your head: Will we be replaced by AI?

It’s not an easy question.

History shows that some roles can vanish as technology evolves. Think of switchboard operators, once essential for connecting phone calls, or lamplighters, who lit and maintained gas street lamps before electric lighting—both replaced by automation.

At the same time, technological evolution creates entirely new roles that didn’t exist before. Software developers and programmers, for instance, only came into existence with computers. Social media managers now shape online presence for brands, data scientists analyze massive datasets, and drone operators handle photography, delivery, inspections, and other commercial tasks that were impossible just a few years ago.

The lesson is clear: technology changes the landscape, sometimes replacing roles, sometimes creating them. What I do think is that as of now, AI models still need guidance and supervision, but when used well, they can genuinely augment our work—helping us avoid mistakes, catch issues early, and move faster than ever before.

I also found that when an LLM keeps iterating on a problem without making real progress, it’s often just shooting in the dark. At that point, a human intervention is usually the better choice.

Feeling augmented can be incredibly fulfilling, to the point of wanting to do more and more. But this can easily increase context switching, which for us humans is particularly costly. Finding the right balance, and avoiding overdoing it, becomes essential.

That said, if you’re still on JUnit 4, you really don’t have any excuses these days!

entry.title: Debezium 3.4.0.Final Released
entry.content:
As we close our 2025 and the team takes a well deserved break for the holidays with friends and family, we’re pleased to announce the immediate availability of Debezium 3.4.0.Final, the next minor release milestone. This release includes over 125 new features, improvements, and fixes across the entire Debezium project portfolio.

In this post, we’re going to take a deep dive into all the changes in Debezium 3.4, discussing new features, and explaining all the possible changes that could have any impact to your upgrade process. As always, we recommend you read the release notes to learn about all the bugs that were fixed, update procedures, and more.

  • Breaking changes

  • New features and improvements

  • Other changes

  • What’s next?

Breaking changes

With any new release of software, there is often several breaking changes. This release is no exception, so let’s discuss the major changes you should be aware of before upgrading to Debezium 3.3.0.Final.

Debezium for IBMi

Debezium for Oracle

Debezium for PostgreSQL

Debezium for SQL Server

Debezium for IBMi

String-based default values trimmed automatically

The IBMi connector will now automatically trim both leading and trailing whitespaces for string-based fields that have default values. In previous versions, trimming was not performed and the default value was provided as maintained by the database.

We understand that this behavior change may not be desired in all environments, and therefore it can be customized. A new configuration property trim.non.xml.charsequence.field.mode can be used to adjust the behavior as needed (DBZ-8835).

both

The connector default behavior, which will trim both leading and trailing whitespaces.

leading

The connector will trim leading whitespaces only.

trailing

The connector will trim trailing whitespaces only.

none

The connector will not perform any whitespace trimming. This option should be used if you wish to preserve the older connector behavior during the upgrade process.

Debezium for Oracle

XML dependencies included by default

The Debezium Oracle connector now ships with the XDB and XMLParserV2 libraries as part of the community plugin distribution artifacts. This simplifies the process for capturing XML column types as community users no longer need to download and install these dependencies separately (DBZ-9587).

Debezium for PostgreSQL

PostgreSQL 13 support has ended

With PostgreSQL 13 being sunset, the Debezium project will no longer test nor support PostgreSQL 13 in this and future releases (DBZ-9376). While Debezium frequently sunsets support for older database versions, most often Debezium remains compatible with these older database versions for extended periods of time.

Configurable flush strategy changes

A new configuration option was added for PostgreSQL users called lsn.flush.mode. This option provides more control over the replication slot flush strategy (DBZ-9641). This configuration option replaces flush.lsn.source, which is now deprecated and will be removed in a future update.

Debezium for SQL Server

Streaming query mode changed

In previous builds, the SQL Server connector used function as the default value for data.query.mode. This meant that Debezium relied on SQL Server’s built-in functions to provide the list of changes for a given table.

The default for data.query.mode has changed in Debezium 3.4, and is now direct (DBZ-9394). This uses a more efficient query that is built by Debezium for collecting changes for tables.

If you would like to restore the old behavior, please set data.query.mode to function in your connector configuration.

New features and improvements

The following describes all noteworthy new features and improvements in Debezium 3.4.0.Final. For a complete list, be sure to read the release notes for more details.

Debezium Core

Debezium for IBMi

Debezium for MongoDB

Debezium for Oracle

Debezium for PostgreSQL

Debezium for Quarkus

Debezium for SQL Server

Debezium for Vitess

Debezium JDBC sink

Debezium Server

Debezium Core

Kafka 4.1.1 support

Debezium 3.4 is based on the latest stable release of Kafka, version 4.1.1 (DBZ-9709), released in November 2025. Kafka has fixed KAFKA-19758, a class loading regression reported by the Debezium community, that prevented Debezium from working with Kafka 4.1.

Please be sure to avoid updating to Kafka 4.1.0. We recommend anyone who intends to update your Kafka ecosystem while staying on older Debezium builds, skip 4.1.0 and go directly to 4.1.1.

Debezium 3.4.0.Final or later is required if you intend to target Kafka 4.1.0 and not 4.1.1 or later.

OpenLineage improvements

Several users reported issues when openlineage.integration.enabled was set to false, Debezium was still trying to resolve OpenLineage features. This could lead to undesirable IllegalStateException errors while trying to initialize OpenLineage, although it was not enabled.

Debezium now respects the openlineage.integration.enabled configuration property and will no longer attempt to perform any OpenLineage setup or initialization when set to false (DBZ-9504).

Additionally, we have made several changes to how OpenLineage transforms manage state to minimize the impact of the class loading regression KAFKA-19758. If your Kafka ecosystem must use Kafka 4.1.0, Debezium 3.4+ will be required to work correctly with Kafka 4.1.0 (DBZ-9541).

Large schema memory guards

For every table that a connector maintains schema history for and/or captures, Debezium maintains a model in-memory that describes the primary keys, columns, column types, and other attributes after the table. In large environments where a connector is managing hundreds to tens of thousands of tables, the memory footprint for the in-memory relational model can be quite large.

To address these concerns, users can opt-in and configure limits to minimize the potential for OutOfMemoryError issues (DBZ-9427). These new configuration properties include the following:

guardrail.collections.max

Specifies the maximum number of tables that the connector can capture. Exceeding this limit triggers the action specified by guardrail.collections.limit.action. Setting this property to 0 (the default) prevents the connector from triggering the guardrail action.

guardrail.collections.limit.action

Specifies the action to trigger if the number of tables that the connector captures exceeds the number specified in guardrails.collections.max. The property can be set to fail to report an exception or warn (the default) to log a warning.

These settings help avoid misconfigurations or malicious setups that lead to downtime or memory issues. These are particularly useful for end users who want to avoid accidental crashes or for managed service vendors who use Debezium to minimize infrastructure risks.

New geometry coordinate system swap transformation

Not every source uses the same coordinate system to represent geometry and geography data. In some sources, they prefer (longitude latitude) while others prefer (latitude longitude), similarly to (x y) versus (y x).

This inconsistency is prevalent in databases when replicating geometry data, so it’s critical to understand not only how the source serializes the data, but equally important how the target database expects the coordinates to be provided. For example, if your source uses (x y), and the target database expects (y x), incorrectly serializing the data to the target database will mean applications that read the geometry data will have inverted coordinates.

To make working with geometry data easier and to avoid needing to convert the byte data manually, Debezium introduces a new SwapGeometryCoordinates transformation specifically for this purpose (DBZ-9556). This transform is extremely important when you are emitting geometry data from one source like PostgreSQL and writing the data to Oracle where they use opposite coordinate systems.

Example connector transform configuration
{
  "transforms": "swapcoords",
  "transforms.swapcoords.type": "io.debezium.transforms.SwapGeometryCoordinates",
  "transforms.swapcoords.srids": "4326,3857,4269"
}

By default, the transform will only swap the coordinates for geometry fields with a spatial reference identifier of 4326, 3857, or 4269. The list of spatial reference identifiers can be adjusted to your needs through configuration.

The transformation is designed to swap the coordinates for all encoded geometry types as long as the spatial reference identifier in the field’s Struct matches on of the spatial references in the SRID list. It’s the sole responsibility of the user to understand the differences in the coordinate systems used by the source and target to determine if the transformation is necessary.

New Geometry format conversion transformation

The new GeometryFormatTransformer transformation allows for the conversion of io.debezium.data.Geometry or io.debezium.data.Geography logical types between Well-Known Binary (WKB) and Extended Well-Know Binary (EWKB) formats (DBZ-9575). To get started with this transformation, simply add it to your connector configuration

Example connector transform configuration
{
  "transforms": "geo-format",
  "transforms.geo-format.type": "io.debezium.transforms.GeometryFormatTransformer",
  "transforms.geo-format.format": "WKB"
}

In the above example, if a geometry logical type field contains serialized bytes using the EWKB format, that value will be converted to use WKB instead. See the documentation for more details.

Timezone conversion support for source info block fields

The ConvertTimezone SMT has been a great addition for specific use cases where the community has wanted to shift the values of timestamps by timezone offsets. However, this transformation’s capabilities were limited to very specific Debezium logical field types.

A common community request was to extend the transformation to support additional fields in the event’s source information block. In Debezium 3.4, the ts_ms, ts_us, and ts_ns fields from the source information block are eligible fields that can be converted (DBZ-9372).

Please see the ConvertTimezone documentation for more details.

Debezium for IBMi

Incremental snapshot support

The incremental snapshot feature is an integral part of Debezium’s toolkit, which allows for on-demand, concurrent, resumable, and targeted snapshot/backfill of historical data for one or more tables (DBZ-7958). In Debezium 3.4, this feature is now supported by the Debezium for IBMi connector.

Multi-journal support

The IBMi database allows for the assignment of different journals to multiple tables under the same schema. To address this unique database behavior and to provide sufficient context for correctly ordering events across a database, the IBMi connector’s source information block now includes information about the journals receiver file name, receiver library, entry’s timestamp, and sequence number (DBZ-9291).

Debezium for MongoDB

Support MongoDB wall clock time

In MongoDB 6+, wallTime was added to MongoDB change stream events to represent the server’s date and time when a database operation occurred, specifically when the transaction was committed or the operation completed. This is slightly different from clusterTime, which is when the entry was added to the database’s oplog.

Starting with Debezium 3.4, the ts_ms, ts_us, and ts_ns source information block fields will be based on the wallTime if it’s available in the change event. If the wallTime is unavailable, the connector will fall back to clusterTime (DBZ-9683).

Debezium for Oracle

LogMiner metrics improvements

We have added and adjusted several Oracle LogMiner JMX metrics to provide better information and clarify about the connector’s health and performance.

Commit throughput and related metrics changes

Previously, the LogMiner CommitThroughput JMX metric was calculated over the connector’s entire runtime, which meant extended periods of inactivity would progressively reduce the reported throughput value. This approach proved unhelpful for users trying to gauge the actual throughput achieved during active change emission from Oracle’s transaction buffer to Kafka.

To address this, the calculation of CommiThroughput has changed to focus exclusively on the commit duration window, delivering a more precise measure of the connector’s capacity to queue changes for Kafka delivery (DBZ-9639).

A declining value over time may indicate that your QueueRemainingCapacity has hit 0, suggesting you should consider adjusting the outbound queue configuration or review your throughput to your target system.

Additionally, to align with metrics from other LogMiner processing stages, we’ve introduced a new JMX metric named TotalCommitTimeInMilliseconds. This metric tracks the aggregate time spent executing the commit loop since the connector’s current startup (DBZ-9637).

New metrics

In some troubleshooting scenarios, it’s often useful to understand what redo log positions are used by Debezium’s Oracle connector. To obtain this information requires increasing the connector’s logging verbosity, which is not always feasible in a production environment.

In addition, Debezium introduced a separation between the mining log range and the data read range to improve performance and address a number of outstanding issues in DBZ-8747 for the LogMiner adapter. To compliment that change, we have added these ranges to the existing breadth of connector streaming metrics.

Metric Name Type Description

MiningSessionLowerBounds

BigInteger

The system change number used as the LogMiner session lower boundary.

MiningSessionUpperBounds

BigInteger

The system change number used as the LogMiner session upper boundary.

MiningFetchLowerBounds

BigInteger

The system change number currently used as the LogMiner fetch query lower boundary.

MiningFetchUpperBounds

BigInteger

The system change number currently used as the LogMiner fetch query upper boundary.

The MiningSession* metrics represent the range that redo logs are gathered between while the MiningFetch* metrics represent the range Debezium requests to read the redo logs. While Debezium may request a specific range, LogMiner may opt to read outside the fetch range but within the session range to satisfy transaction stitching needs.

Subset database replication supported

Debezium has long recommended that the best supplemental logging configuration is to enable minimum supplemental logging mode at the database level and use granular "all column" logging per table. This minimizes the volume of data recorded in your database transaction logs and improves the overall performance of Debezium.

In Oracle 21, a new supplemental logging mode was introduced called SUBSET DATABASE REPLICATION, which acts as a replacement for the previously used Minimum Supplemental Logging Mode. This new logging more is now recognized and treated as an equivalent to the minimal supplemental logging mode, allowing users to set one or the other rather than both (DBZ-7341), simplifying the setup required for capturing changes using LogMiner.

Manually discard in-progress transactions via signals

The Oracle connector is a bit unique in that it must buffer all events for a transaction before the transaction can be emitted as change events when using LogMiner. In some situations, users have found where a large or long-running transaction is being buffered, but it’s not changing any tables that are being captured. Currently, you need to wait for the transaction commit or rollback to be observed or the transaction buffer retention to be met.

A new Oracle-specific signal called drop-transaction can be used to specifically discard an in-progress transaction (DBZ-9552).

Example discard transaction signal
INSERT INTO the_signal_table
VALUES ('my-signal-id', 'drop-transaction', '{"transaction-id": "<the-database-trx-id>"}');

When this signal is processed, Debezium will locate the transaction in the buffer, and if it exists, the transaction will be abandoned immediately rather than waiting for the transaction buffer retention if configured.

Configurable LogMiner performance options

An Oracle database is configured by database administrators with a variety of session default values. Many of these settings control a variety of session behaviors, including the amount of resources the connection can consume when executing queries or running PL/SQL programs. Two most notable database parameters are:

hash_area_size

This specifies the maximum amount of memory, in bytes, to be used when performing hash joins.

sort_area_size

This specifies the maximum amount of memory, in bytes, to be used when performing query sorts.

Normally these values are set automatically by the database sizing configuration and should not be altered. However, there are some corner cases where adjusting these values can help improve specific queries and performance, including the log mining pass used by Debezium.

To adjust these two options, the Debezium Oracle connector provides two internal, experimental properties:

internal.log.mining.hash.area.size

Specifies the maximum amount of memory, in bytes, to be used for hash joins.

internal.log.mining.sort.area.size

Specifies the maximum amount of memory, in bytes, to be used for query sorts.

Careful consideration should be taken before setting these configuration options. In situations where these values are set too large, this can create stability issues in the database.

You should consult your database administrator before setting these.

Performance improvements

When an Oracle LogMiner mining step completes, the connector needs to calculate the next starting position for mining. When lob.enabled is set to false (the default), it was observed that this calculation was too conservative, and could lead to a regression in performance. This regression affected a variety of Debezium 3.2, 3.3, and 3.4 preview builds.

The connector should once again resume reading changes without the low watermark calculation causing performance loss (DBZ-9664). This fix has been included in Debezium 3.4.0.Final, 3.3.2.Final, and 3.2.5.Final.

Heartbeats no longer stop when using CTE queries

The Debezium Oracle connector recently introduced an experimental feature using Common Table Expression (CTE) queries to allow another way to optimize the data fetch from Oracle LogMiner. However, the community reported that when using this feature, if the query returned no events, Debezium stopped emitting heartbeat events.

This has been fixed, and users should observe that heartbeat events should always be emitted by the Oracle connector, even if the mining pass fetched no data (DBZ-9443).

Active transaction identifiers included in stale offset warning

When the Oracle connector writes to the log file, "Offset SCN X has not advanced in Y mining sessions…​", users are often concerned about what this means and exactly do they determine what transactions are active.

This log message was adjusted to not only make it clearer, but to include all the current active transaction identifiers, making it easy for users to work with their DBA team to understand why there are long-running transactions (debezium/dbz#20).

The log message will now read, "Offset SCN X has not changed in Y mining session iterations. This may indicate long-running transaction(s), active transactions: <list of transaction ids>. Commit SCN: <commit details>".

Transaction retention improvements

For users who use log.mining.transaction.retention.ms, there was an issue that indicated after transactions were evicted from the buffer due to the retention policy, the connector was not properly calculating several key metrics and values (DBZ-9659). This specific regression led to several metrics to report incorrect values, and moreover to LogMiner re-reading data that it should have otherwise skipped.

While this did not introduce any data issues, it did introduce a performance penality that could add up over time in high-traffic systems that we’re happy to have resolved.

Debezium for PostgreSQL

Support for PostgreSQL 18

The next major milestone for the PostgreSQL database was released in September 2025, version 18.0. We’re pleased to announce that Debezium is now tested and compatible with PostgreSQL 18 (DBZ-9523).

AWS IAM authentication support

You can now specify user credentials that will be validated using the AWS AIM authentication process. This feature, while present for MySQL, is now available for PostgreSQL connector users.

Prerequisites

  • Add the AWS Advanced JDBC Wrapper to your connector’s plugin directory or class path.
    You can find more information about this process here.

  • Add the connector configuration property database.connection.factory.class in the connector configuration.
    Set the value to io.debezium.connector.postgresql.connection.PostgresAwsIamConnectionFactory.

With this configuration, the connector credentials will be validated against AWS IAM rather than the database (DBZ-7297).

Improved LSN flushing strategy

In previous versions, users often let Debezium control when the LSN was flushed to the replication slot using flush.lsn.source; however, users could set this false and control the flush manually outside of Debezium.

To expand on this functionality, a new connector configuration lsn.flush.mode was added to provide an extended ways to control how the LSN is flushed to PostgreSQL during the connector’s lifecycle (DBZ-9641). This new property can be set to one of the following options:

connector

Specifies that the Debezium PostgreSQL connector controls when the LSN is flushed to the replication slot. This is the same behavior as the deprecated flush.lsn.source option when set to true.

manual

Specifies that the Debezium PostgreSQL connector no longer controls when the LSN is flushed to the replication slot and that it must be performed manually or externally to the connector. This is the same behavior as the deprecated flush.lsn.source option when set to false.

connector_and_driver

Specifies a new mode where both the Debezium PostgreSQL connector and the PostgreSQL JDBC driver manage when the LSN is flushed to the replication slot. Debezium will flush as it processes events while the driver will flush during idle periods based on the server keepalive messages.

The flush.lsn.source configuration option is deprecated, and will be removed in a future release. Please be sure to adjust your configuration accordingly if using the old option.

Debezium for Quarkus

Debezium as a Quarkus DevService

One of the biggest features of this release includes the new Debezium Quarkus Extension modules. The extension modules provide a complete change data capture solution using Quarkus techniques and best practices, and most importantly, this can all be done as a native application!

Our initial debut of this feature includes support for PostgreSQL (DBZ-8902), MongoDB (DBZ-9432), MySQL (DBZ-9380), MariaDB (DBZ-9381), and SQL Server (DBZ-9384) connectors. For other database platforms, those are planned and you should see those phased in throughout the early part of 2026.

To get started using Debezium as a Quarkus DevService, the specific connector dependency needs to be added to your Quarkus application’s dependencies. Depending on your Quarkus version, these dependencies may be part of the existing Quarkus BOM, but if they are not, you can add these manually.

Example adding a connector dependency
<dependency>
  <groupId>io.debezium.quarkus</groupId>
  <artifactId>quarkus-debezium-mongodb</artifactId>
  <version>3.4.0.Final</version>
</dependency>

With the dependency added to your Quarkus project, you can now use the extension to capture changes with just a few configuration properties in your application.properties file, e.g.

Example MongoDB configuration in application.properties
quarkus.debezium.devservices.mongodb.enabled=true

quarkus.debezium.offset.storage=org.apache.kafka.connect.storage.MemoryOffsetBackingStore
quarkus.debezium.name=native
quarkus.debezium.topic.prefix=integration
quarkus.debezium.database.include.list=test
quarkus.debezium.snapshot.mode=initial
quarkus.mongodb.connection-string=mongodb://native:native@127.0.0.1:27017/?replicaSet=rs0

Capturing changes from MongoDB as simple as creating a Quarkus bean with the right annotations.

Quarkus Debezium MongoDB change event bean
@ApplicationScoped
public class MongoDbChangeEventHandler {
    @Capturing
    public void handleChanges(RecordChangeEvent<SourceRecord> event) throws Exception {
        // your custom change event handler logic
    }
}

Multiple Debezium DevServices in a Quarkus application

In a Quarkus application, users can read data from multiple sources using a variety of Quarkus ready services, such as Hibernate using JPA. So it raises a very valid question, why can’t Debezium’s Quarkus extension services?

In Debezium 3.4, this is now a reality!

In a single Quarkus application using Debezium’s Quarkus extension, you can now capture changes from two or more independent Debezium connector services. This enables a variety of application use cases, e.g., where data is aggregated to produce a data stream for warehousing or caches. It can also be used to publish or emit enriched events from those multiple sources to any number of consumers or consumer types.

To get started, annotate your event observers using the @Engine annotation or @DefaultEngine annotation, e.g.

Example snapshot event listeners
@ApplicationScoped
public class DefaultSnapshotEventObserver {
  public void handleSnapshotEvent(@Observes @Engine("default") SnapshotEvent event) {
  }
}

@ApplicationScoped
public class AlternativeSnapshotEventObserver {
  public void handleSnapshotEvent(@Observers @Engine("alternative") SnapshotEvent event) {
  }
}

With this pattern, multiple Debezium configurations can be added to your application.properties using the standard Quarkus naming pattern, e.g.

Example application.properties
quarkus.debezium.name=native-default
quarkus.debezium.topic.prefix=default
quarkus.debezium.plugin.name=pgoutput
quarkus.debezium.snapshot.mode=initial
quarkus.datasource.db-kind=postgresql
quarkus.datasource.username=native
quarkus.datasource.password=native
quarkus.datasource.jdbc.url=jdbc:postgresql://localhost:5432/native

quarkus.debezium.capturing.alternative.name=native-alternative
quarkus.debezium.capturing.alternative.topic.prefix=alt
quarkus.debezium.capturing.alternative.plugin.name=pgoutput
quarkus.debezium.capturing.alternative.snapshot.mode=initial
quarkus.datasource.alternative.db-kind=postgresql
quarkus.datasource.alternative.username=native
quarkus.datasource.alternative.password=native
quarkus.datasource.alternative.jdbc.url=jdbc:postgresql://localhost:5432/native-alt

quarkus.datasource.devservices.enabled=false

In this trivial example, we’ve configured two independent data sources, each used by different Debezium Quarkus extension instances running all within the same Quarkus application.

What makes this feature really useful is that while the trivial example gathers changes from two independent PostgreSQL databases, the same can be done across database vendor boundaries. By using two or more source connector extensions, you can gather changes from different vendor sources and handle those streams however you like.

When using the Multiple Debezium DevService feature in your Quarkus applications, please note that if you are capturing changes from two independent vendor sources, all connector components must use the same base Debezium version.

In other words, it’s not possible to use Debezium 3.4 for MySQL while using Debezium 3.3 for PostgreSQL within the same Quarkus application.

Debezium for SQL Server

Incremental snapshots now resume after restart

When an incremental snapshot was in progress for a SQL Server connector, if a rebalance or connector restart was triggered for any reason, any in-progress incremental snapshot would fail to resume upon restart. This is unintended and was due to regression in the handling of the connector’s offsets during incremental snapshots.

This issue is fixed for SQL Sever, and we identified that no other connector was impacted by this regression. SQL Server users should now observe that if the connector is restarted during an incremental snapshot, the snapshot resumes upon restart as intended (DBZ-9533).

Multitask signaling support

The Debezium SQL Server connector is the only core relational source connector that supports the ability to capture changes from multiple databases on a shared instance using multiple tasks. This deployment model provides for an efficient CDC solution that uses different tasks for different databases, using a single connector deployment. Unfortunately, not all of Debezium’s advanced features were supported in this mode.

It is now possible when using a multitask connector deployment for SQL Server, signals can be used reliably (DBZ-7243). This allows triggering adhoc blocking or incremental snapshots with this deployment configuration.

Debezium for Vitess

Exclude keyspace from table name in Vitess for improved performance

The Debezium Vitess connector now permits users to exclude the keyspace from the table name by setting the vitess.exclude.keyspace.from.table.name configuration property. When set to true, the keyspace is excluded from the table name which boosts the VTGate performance significantly, which avoids copying each event unnecessarily before they’re sent to Debezium (DBZ-9522).

This feature should be used only when streaming from one keyspace, which is currently the only supported mode of operation.

Debezium JDBC sink

Field name transformation reliably adjusts all fields

The JDBC sink transformation FieldNameTransformation unfortunately was not apply the desired case to all field names in the payload. This led to sporadic reports where the JDBC sink would report the column names were not adjusted by the transformation and that the columns could not be found in the target table (DBZ-9747).

This regression is now fixed and the transform accounts for all use cases correctly.

Geometry data type support

Debezium’s source connectors have had long-standing support for various geometry and geography column types. These types are serialized using custom Debezium logical types based on Kafka’s semantic type Struct. This is a complex field type that allows Debezium to encode both the Well Known Binary (or Extended Well Known Binary) WKB/EWKB byte array along with the spatial reference identifier or SRID.

When pairing Debezium’s JDBC sink with a source connector, the JDBC sink connector will seamlessly convert geometry column values to the target database’s desired format if it supports such column types (DBZ-9508). This new feature is available out of the box with no special configuration.

New passthrough collection naming strategy

The JDBC sink connector is intended to consume Debezium change events without using the ExtractNewRecordState transformation. However, when applying other transformations that are not designed to handle Debezium’s nested event structure, it’s often required so that additional transformations can be applied accurately.

This often creates a challenge because the ExtractNewRecordState removes the source information block from the event structure. This prevents the use of ${source.*} pattern inside the collection.naming.format, limiting your options when mapping events to tables.

To solve this issue, a new passthrough collection naming strategy is included with the JDBC sink connector (DBZ-9679).

This strategy uses the event’s topic name directly, without any sanitization, as the target table name. This allows you to pair any other transformations that modify the event’s structure, including the ability to modify the topic name in-flight, so you have precise control over how events are mapped to tables.

To enable the passthrough collection naming strategy, add this to your connector configuration:

How to configure the passthrough collection naming strategy
{
  "collection.naming.strategy": "io.debezium.sink.naming.PassthroughCollectionNamingStrategy"
}

In this example, events from topic public.orders will be written directly to a table named public.orders.

Debezium Server

OpenLineage output datasets

OpenLineage is an open framework for data lineage collection and analysis. Its purpose is to track metadata about datasets giving information needed to help identify the root cause of complexities often present in change data capture pipelines.

Debezium’s source connectors have support for OpenLineages using a transformation while deployed on Kafka Connect. To simply the process to integrate with OpenLineage, Debezium Server natively provides the integration out of the box without the need to configure a separate transformation (DBZ-9059).

The following example configuration shows how easy it is to get started.

Example Debezium Server application.properties
# Standard Debezium configuration here
...

# OpenLineage configuration
debezium.source.openlineage.integration.enabled=true
debezium.source.openlineage.integration.job.tags=env=prod,team=cdc
debezium.source.openlineage.integration.job.description=This connector does cdc for products
debezium.source.openlineage.integration.job.owers=Mario=maintainer,John Doe=Data scientist
debezium.source.openlineage.integration.config.file.path=<path>/debezium-openlineage.yml
Example debezium-openlineage.yml
transport:
  type: debezium

Azure Event Hubs dynamic partition routing

Debezium 3.2 introduced a new dynamic partitioning mechanism that inadvertently disrupted the PartitionRouting transformation’s capability to pre-generate partition identifiers for Event Hubs publishing in specific scenarios. To resolve this issue, we’ve added a new configuration option called debezium.sink.eventhubs.dynamicpartitionrouting (DBZ-9572) that accepts one of the following values:

default

If the event has a key, uses the hash algorithm to compute the partition based on the event key; otherwise when there is no key, falls back to using the partitionId strategy.

key

If the event has a key, uses the hash algorithm to compute the partition based on the event key; otherwise falls back to the batch index for non partition id.

partitionid

Will use the event’s computed partition if present, otherwise falls back to the batch index for non partition id.

Other fixes

The following are just a subset of some noteworthy additional changes and fixes in Debezium 3.4:

  • Can bind a LONG value only for insert into a LONG column DBZ-8276

  • Debezium db2i CDC source connector randomly loses Events DBZ-8538

  • Oracle Connector stops mining on REVOKE FLASHBACK on …​ DBZ-9112

  • Support Redis Cluster mode in the Debezium Redis sink module DBZ-9226

  • Align Debezium Oracle DDL grammar with upstream DBZ-9302

  • Provide the table explorer table component DBZ-9318

  • Apply query.fetch.size universally to all Oracle non-snapshot queries DBZ-9448

  • Apply mining upper boundary to avoid PGA_AGGREGATE_LIMIT DBZ-9476

  • Debezium platform conductor service fails on /q/openapi DBZ-9496

  • Use Jakarta variant of ehcache DBZ-9517

  • Only log an error when the dump folder is provided but doesn’t exist DBZ-9519

  • Events are mistakenly skipped during commit dispatch when LOB is enabled DBZ-9521

  • Missing OpenLineage Complete event during gracefully shutdown DBZ-9524

  • Support TOKENLIST datatype in Spanner connector DBZ-9526

  • Correct type is not used for the PORT field in the connection payload DBZ-9530

  • Add support to show the Active count in the Connection page DBZ-9531

  • Oracle alter DDL to move partition/subpartition fails to be parsed DBZ-9534

  • SchemaUtil creates invalid JSON DBZ-9540

  • Pipeline page Issues DBZ-9543

  • Deadlock due to lost interrupt with blc keep alive thread DBZ-9548

  • DdlChanges not reset in schema history recovery DBZ-9549

  • Timestamp values cause NPE in Postgres on JDK23+ DBZ-9558

  • Handle the form properties with dot present in their name DBZ-9560

  • Add basic UI validation in the Pipeline package specific log configuration options DBZ-9561

  • Send the signal.data.collection property in the source payload only when its added DBZ-9562

  • Skipped events counter not handled correctly for compressed transactions DBZ-9564

  • Update MongoDB driver to 5.5.1 DBZ-9585

  • Fix failed to initialize open lineage for vitess connector DBZ-9613

  • Fix minor issues in the Platform UI dark mode DBZ-9633

  • MongoDB connector: Whitespace in collection.include.list causes incorrect regex pattern in change streams DBZ-9657

  • Debezium Oracle restarting mining session too frequently DBZ-9680

  • Snapshot SQL Override Spaces DBZ-9695

  • Debezium Cassandra Connector Silently Stops Processing After CommitLog Move Failure DBZ-9710

  • PostgreSQL Connector: Keep-alive thread logs ERROR on normal shutdown due to InterruptedException debezium/dbz#14
