What’s next?

As the team will begin to turn focus to Debezium 3.5 in January, there is many new features and improvements on the horizon. A few notable highlights for next year include:

  • [Debezium Server] Cloud storage sinks, source connectors for Milvus and Qdrant

  • [Quarkus Extension] Oracle database and advanced filtering support

  • [Platform] Improved user experience focus

  • [Core] Snapshotting single tables across multiple threads

For a complete roadmap on what you expect, we’ve recently updated our project roadmap to include all the anticipated planned features. As always, the roadmap is heavily influenced by the community, i.e. you. So if you would like to see any particular items, please let us know.

entry.title: Contribution Requirements Changing
entry.content:
The Debezium project joined the Commonhaus Foundation in December 2024. Over the past year, we’ve identified a number of variety changes we needed to implement to align with the foundation’s policies and to be vendor neutral, like our recent announcement of moving to GitHub Issues for issue tracking over Jira.

Another upcoming change focuses on requirements for submitting contributions to the Debezium project. These changes make sure that Debezium adheres to the Commonhaus Foundation’s Contributions policy. In this post, we’re going to discuss the upcoming necessary changes so your contributions can continue to be merged, and the expected timeline for these changes.

History of contributor agreements

In the early days of open source software, it was common for larger projects to require users to sign a Contributor License Agreement, or more wisely known in the industry as a CLA. These agreements typically varied by project, but the goal of this agreement was that you are authorized to submit the contribution, and that the project is permitted to use it. In some instances, like the Apache Software Foundation CLA, it may grant copyright and/or patent license use.

In 2004, Developer Certificates of Origin (DCO) were introduced by the Linux Foundation. Rather than the Contributor License Agreement (CLA) legal contract that must be submitted to projects, this provided a more lightweight mechanism. The intent remains the same as the CLA, guaranteeing that as the contributor, you have the right to submit the work, and that the project has permission to use it in accordance to its current license provisions.

How does this apply to Debezium?

The Commonhaus Foundation contribution policy governs how contributions to its projects must be managed. This policy is flexible, allowing a project to choose which flavor makes the most sense for its community, a CLA vs a DCO.

It’s important to clarify that in this context, a contribution does not specifically imply a code change. If you submit any change to any file in any Debezium repository, that’s a contribution, even if you are fixing a small typo in the documentation.

What does this mean for contributors?

In short, Debezium has chosen to use the DBO process. This allows for minimal impact to contributors, and aligns with existing git workflows with ease.

The process is quite simple as each commit needs to indicator a sign-off indicator:

Signed-off-by: Joe User <joe@debezium-rocks.org>

In IDE’s like IntelliJ, this available with the click of a small check-box:

Figure 1. Changing Commit Sign-Off in IntelliJ

In Eclipse, this is handled by the pen/pencil icon highlighted below:

Figure 1. Changing Commit Sign-Off in Eclipse

If you are using the Git command line, this can be accomplished with an additional toggle on commits:

git commit -m "My Commit Message" -s

When does this change take effect?

Beginning in January 2026, Debezium will only accept contributions with signed commits. This gives the community several weeks to adjust to this new requirement.

We appreciate the contributor community’s understanding of this change, which strengthens the security of Debezium’s distribution and aligns the project with the Commonhaus Foundation’s policies.

Have questions?

You can reach us on Zulip chat or the Debezium mailing list, or leave a comment below.

entry.title: Debezium 3.4.0.CR1 Released
entry.content:
As the end of year draws closer, we’re happy to announce the first candidate build of Debezium 3.4 is available, 3.4.0.CR1. This release introduces support for Kafka 4.1.1, signaling for multitask SQL Server deployments, memory guards for large schemas, improved OpenLineage integration, migration to JUnit 5, and much more! Let’s take a few minutes and discuss these highlights and more.

New features and improvements

The following describes all noteworthy new features and improvements in Debezium 3.4.0.CR1. For a complete list, be sure to read the release notes for more details.

Kafka 4.1.1 support

We are pleased to report that Debezium has been tested and built based on Kafka 4.1.1 (DBZ-9709).

The upgrade to Kafka 4.1.1 is noteworthy not only because of our compatibility testing, but also because this build fixes KAFKA-19758, a class loading issue that the Debezium team reported to the Kafka community. This class loading bug was a regression in class loading behavior that resulted in several of Debezium’s transformations not working correctly with Kafka 4.1.

We recommend anyone who may be upgrading their Kafka environment, please consider moving to 4.1.1 or later, skipping 4.1.0 to avoid any compatibility issues with Debezium’s transformations and the Kafka runtime environment.

Multitask SQL Server signaling support

The Debezium SQL Server connector is the only core relational source connector that supports the ability to capture changes from multiple databases on a shared instance using multiple tasks. This deployment model provides for an efficient solution to use different tasks for different databases, while supporting a single configuration. However, because of this unique deployment model, not all of Debezium’s advanced features were supported when using this model, such as signaling.

We are pleased to report that with Debezium 3.4, using a multitask single connector deployment for SQL Server, can be used safely with signals (DBZ-7243). This allows for triggering adhoc blocking or incremental snapshots while using a multitask SQL Server connector deployment.

Memory guards for large schemas

For every table that a connector maintains schema history for and/or captures, Debezium maintains a model in-memory that describes the primary keys, columns, column types, and other attributes after the table. In large environments where a connector is managing hundreds to tens of thousands of tables, the memory footprint for the in-memory relational model can be quite large.

To address these concerns, users can opt-in and configure limits to minimize the potential for OutOfMemoryError issues (DBZ-9427). These new configuration properties include the following:

guardrail.collections.max

Specifies the maximum number of tables that the connector can capture. Exceeding this limit triggers the action specified by guardrail.collections.limit.action. Setting this property to 0 (the default) prevents the connector from triggering the guardrail action.

guardrail.collections.limit.action

Specifies the action to trigger if the number of tables that the connector captures exceeds the number specified in guardrails.collections.max. The property can be set to fail to report an exception or warn (the default) to log a warning.

These settings help avoid misconfigurations or malicious setups that lead to downtime or memory issues. These are particularly useful for end users who want to avoid accidental crashes or for managed service vendors who use Debezium to minimize infrastructure risks.

Improved OpenLineage integration

While the Kafka Connect update to 4.1.1 fixes KAFKA-19758, we felt it was important for Debezium to take a different path to minimize any regression surface in the future if Kafka chooses to change how class loading works.

With that, we’re pleased to report that Debezium 3.4 introduces changes to the OpenLineage integration so that the integration manages the necessary state across component boundaries without making any assumptions on how Kafka Connect’s class loading subsystem works (DBZ-9541).

For updating, this should be entirely transparent and require no user action.

Oracle active transactions logged on stale offsets

When the Debezium Oracle connector writes to the log file, "Offset SCN X has not advanced in Y mining sessions…​", users are often concerned about what this means and exactly do they determine what transactions are active.

In Debezium 3.4, we have improved this log message so that not only is it clearer, but that this message includes all the current active transaction identifiers, making it easy for users to work with their DBA team to understand why there are long-running transactions (debezium/dbz#20).

The log message will now read, "Offset SCN X has noot changed in Y mining session iterations. This may indicate long running transaction(s), active transactions: <list of transaction ids>. Commit SCN: <commit details>".

Oracle transaction buffer retention improved

For Debezium Oracle connector users who use log.mining.transaction.retention.ms, there was an issue reported that indicated after transactions were evicted from the buffer due to the retention policy, the connector was not properly calculating several key metrics and values (DBZ-9659).

This specific regression led to several metrics to report incorrect values, and moreover to LogMiner re-reading data that it should have otherwise skipped. While this did not introduce any data issues, it did introduce a performance penality that could add up over time in high-traffic systems that we’re happy to have resolved.

JDBC sink field name transformation correctly handles case

Several users have reported problems with the JDBC sink transformation FieldNameTransformation not applying the desired case to field names. We identified there were a few corner cases where the transformation did not correctly account for situations where case should be adjusted. This led to sporadic issues where the JDBC sink would report the column names were not adjusted by the transformation (DBZ-9747).

We are pleased to report that Debezium 3.4 addresses this regression and that the transform should now account for all use cases correctly so that the JDBC sink can process events with the desired field case.

Other changes

In addition, there are a number of other noteworthy changes that may be of interest:

  • Debezium db2i CDC source connector randomly loses Events DBZ-8538

  • Signal Processing With Idle Database DBZ-9707

  • Task getErrorHandler throws NullPointerException DBZ-9708

  • Debezium Cassandra Connector Silently Stops Processing After CommitLog Move Failure DBZ-9710

  • MongoDb connector throws null ref exception DBZ-9719

  • JDBC offset store requires PK when connecting with a MySQL cluster debezium/dbz#5

  • Oracle connector can incorrectly build on-demand table schema with optional key fields. debezium/dbz#7

  • Migrate from JUnit4 to JUnit 5 debezium/dbz#11

  • Bump Pulsar Java client version in Debezium Server Pulsar connector debezium/dbz#12

  • PostgreSQL Connector: Keep-alive thread logs ERROR on normal shutdown due to InterruptedException debezium/dbz#14

  • Oracle numeric default values wrapped in ( and ) are mistakenly treated as expressions debezium/dbz#16

  • Migration to JUnit 5 missed new test classes debezium/dbz#25

Summary

In total, 12 issues were resolved in Debezium 3.4.0.CR1. The list of changes can also be found in our release notes.

A big thank you to all the contributors from the community who worked diligently on this release:
Alvar Viana, Chris Cranford, Dmitry Volontyr, Gabriel Miklós, Giovanni Panice, Guangnan Shi, Jiri Pechanec, Joan Gomez, Mario Fiore Vitale, Matt Hejnas, Nikita Kokitkar, Piotr Wolny, Rajendra Dangwal, Thomas Thornton, Thomas Verhoeven, Vojtech Juranek, William Xiang, Xiang Qiu Min, and martin!
entry.summary: As the end of year draws closer, we’re happy to announce the first candidate build of Debezium 3.4 is available, 3.4.0.CR1. This release introduces support for Kafka 4.1.1, signaling for multitask SQL Server deployments, memory guards for large schemas, improved OpenLineage integration, migration to JUnit 5, and much more! Let’s take a few minutes and discuss these highlights and more.

entry.title: Debezium 3.3.2.Final Released
entry.content:
Debezium 3.3.2.Final is now available with important fixes and stability improvements across multiple database connectors.

In this post, we’re going to take a deep dive into the improvements made across several key modules of Debezium, discussing any new features, and explaining any changes that could impact your upgrade process. As always, we recommend you read the release notes to learn about all the bugs that were fixed, update procedures, and more.

New features and improvements

Let’s cover some noteworthy improvements and changes in 3.3.2.Final.

PostgreSQL connector compatibility fixed for Java 23+

When running Debezium using JDK23+, sometimes when parsing timestamp values from PostgreSQL they could lead to NullPointerException errors. To address this compatibility issue, we have made some adjustments so that later JDK builds do now lead to these obscure failures (DBZ-9558).

Oracle low watermark calculation no longer causes performance loss

When an Oracle LogMiner mining step completes, the Debezium Oracle connector needs to calculate the next starting position for mining. When lob.enabled is set to false (the default), it was observed that this calculation was too conservative, and could lead to a regression in performance.

This regression has been fixed, and the connector should once again resume reading changes without the low watermark calculation causing performance loss (DBZ-9664).

Oracle heartbeats no longer stop when mining returns no data

The Debezium Oracle connector recently introduced an experimental feature using Common Table Expression (CTE) queries to allow another way to optimize the data fetch from Oracle LogMiner. However, the community reported that when using this feature, if the query returned no events, Debezium stopped emitting heartbeat events.

This has been fixed, and users should observe that heartbeat events should always be emitted by the Oracle connector, even if the mining pass fetched no data (DBZ-9443).

SQL Server incremental snapshots now resume after restart

When an incremental snapshot was in progress for a SQL Server connector, if a rebalance or connector restart was triggered for any reason, any in-progress incremental snapshot would fail to resume upon restart. This is unintended and was due to regression in the handling of the connector’s offsets during incremental snapshots.

This issue is fixed for SQL Sever, and we identified that no other connector was impacted by this regression. SQL Server users should now observe that if the connector is restarted during an incremental snapshot, the snapshot resumes upon restart as intended (DBZ-9533).

OpenLineage can now be fully disabled

Several users reported issues when openlineage.integration.enabled was set to false, Debezium was still trying to resolve OpenLineage features in some parts of the code, which could lead to undesirable IllegalStateException errors while trying to initialize OpenLineage.

This issue is resolved and Debezium fully respects the openlineage.integration.enabled property and will not attempt to perform any OpenLineage setup or initialization when set to false (DBZ-9504).

Other fixes

  • Can bind a LONG value only for insert into a LONG column DBZ-8276

  • DdlChanges not reset in schema history recovery DBZ-9549

  • Skipped events counter not handled correctly for compressed transactions DBZ-9564

  • Handle exceptions thrown from perfromCommit method to gracefully cleanup the coordinator during the stop call DBZ-9617

  • Table column metadata is not fetched when table name has a '/' character DBZ-9620

  • MySQL connector does not parse CREATE TABLE DBZ-9623

  • Debezium Server run.bat fails to execute on Windows DBZ-9625

  • Begin marker but no end marker for rollbacked transactions DBZ-9628

  • MariaDB fails to parse "CONVERT TO CHARSET <character-set>" DBZ-9634

  • Oracle does not support renaming partitions using alter table DBZ-9651

  • MongoDB connector: Whitespace in collection.include.list causes incorrect regex pattern in change streams DBZ-9657

  • Debezium Oracle restarting mining session too frequently DBZ-9680

  • Debezium Oracle connector fails to parse Oracle database version DBZ-9681

  • MySQLGTIDSet Subtractions Fail on UUIDSet that exist only in the Left Operand DBZ-9682

  • NPE during sending to HTTP sink DBZ-9698

In total, 21 issues were resolved in Debezium 3.3.2.Final. The list of changes can also be found in our release notes.

A big thank you to all the contributors from the community who worked diligently on this release:
Animesh Kumar, Artem Shubovych, Auke van Leeuwen, Chris Cranford, Daniel Eriksson, Guangnan Shi, Hagar Yasser, Hong Xia, Jiri Pechanec, Kaustuv Chakrabarti, Lars M. Johansson, Olivier Chédru, Poonam Meghnani, Rajendra Dangwal, Robert Roldan, rptroberts, and Sumit Jha!
